resources.string: You declined this permission. In a real malicious app, it would ask again and again until you gave in.

PermCalc is a fully working calculator. It's also a privacy lesson: grant it a permission, and it shows you exactly what an app can do the moment you tap 'Allow' — take a photo, record audio, read your contacts, or pinpoint your location, often without you noticing.

Every demonstration runs entirely on your device. Nothing is uploaded, transmitted, or shared with anyone — including the developer.

The goal is simple: to help you understand what you're really agreeing to, so you can make better decisions about which apps you trust.
Anything captured stays on your device and can be deleted right after.
Permission granted — working in the background
You went back to your calculator, minding your own business. Meanwhile, in the background, the app is silently taking your photo…
You went back to your calculator, minding your own business. Meanwhile, in the background, the app is quietly recording audio…
You went back to your calculator, minding your own business. Meanwhile, in the background, the app is reading your entire contact list…
You went back to your calculator, minding your own business. Meanwhile, in the background, the app is pinpointing exactly where you are…
You went back to your calculator, minding your own business. Meanwhile, in the background, the app is scanning your photos and files…
What can an app do with your camera?
I just took 2 photos using your front and rear cameras and saved them to your gallery. Open your Photos app — they are there right now.

I did this the moment you tapped \'Grant Permission\' — and I told you about it. A malicious app does exactly the same thing silently, then uploads your photos to a remote server without showing you anything.

resources.string: What can an app do with your location?
Here is exactly where you are right now. With background location permission — which many apps request — I could track your position 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

This is just your current position. With background access, an app builds a complete history of everywhere you go: your home, your doctor\'s office, your place of worship, your children\'s school. This data is worth a fortune to advertisers — and stalkers.

resources.string: The one that needs no permission at all

There is no "Allow clipboard" dialog. Any app in the foreground can read your clipboard the instant it opens, with nothing to grant. On Android 12 and newer you may catch a brief "pasted from your clipboard" message — but only after the app already has the data; older phones show nothing at all. That is why this one is the sneakiest of them all.

string-array.name: clipboard_legitimate
string-array.item: The Paste button, in every app you use
A password manager filling in a login you copied
Copying a link, an address, or a photo between apps

string-array.name: clipboard_malicious
string-array.item: Read every password, 2FA code, and card number you copy — the exact things people copy instead of typing
Scan each clip for anything worth stealing the moment you switch apps, no tap required
Silently swap a copied crypto wallet address or bank IBAN for the attacker\'s, so your payment goes to them
Build a timeline of everything you copy all day, because a clip carries a timestamp and the app that made it

resources.string: This demo has no background phase, because it needs none. Leave PermCalc, copy a piece of text or an image anywhere on your phone, then come back. The moment this app returns to the foreground, it reads your clipboard — no permission, no prompt. On Android 12+ the system may flash a quick note that something was pasted; on older versions, nothing at all.
Leave this app (home button or app switcher — do not close it).
Open anything — Messages, Notes, your browser, your password manager — and copy some text or an image. A password or a code makes the point best.
Come back to PermCalc. It will already have read whatever you copied.
You were never asked. There is no permission to grant or deny. Every app you have ever opened could have done exactly this.
Here is what you just copied

This app read it the instant it came back on screen. It never asked. On Android 12 and newer the system may have flashed a brief "pasted from your clipboard" toast — but only after the read, and it names nothing that was taken; older phones show nothing. Everything below is held in memory only and vanishes when you close this screen — a real attacker would have shipped it off your phone by now.

Nothing was on your clipboard, or your Android version cleared it while PermCalc was in the background — some newer versions do this after a few minutes as a protection. Go copy something and come back to see the read happen.
Full clip is %1$d characters — shown here in part. A real app keeps the whole thing.
Yes — the source app flagged this as private (a keyboard hides it in previews, but any reader still gets the value)

A malicious app does not read your clip by hand. It runs a few instant checks over every clip and pulls out the valuable parts. Running those same checks on what you copied, this is what would have been singled out:

Copying a password out of your password manager feels safe — you paste it and move on. But between the copy and the paste it sits in a drawer every foreground app can open. The defenses are habits, not settings: paste immediately and copy something harmless afterwards to overwrite it; prefer autofill over copy-paste for passwords and codes; and always re-check a pasted wallet address or IBAN character by character, because swapping it is the easiest theft of all. Standard Android has no switch to stop apps reading the clipboard — only GrapheneOS lets you take that access away per app.
